I’m French. I want to talk to Americans who are about to vote Democrat. Not to insult you. To warn you.

I come from your future.

In France we did everything your progressive politicians promise. Free healthcare, free college, generous welfare, strong unions, heavy regulation, high taxes on the rich, a state that takes care of everything. Public spending close to 57% of GDP, one of the highest on the planet. On paper, it’s the dream.

Here’s what it looks like from the inside. France hasn’t passed a balanced budget since 1974. Our debt is above 3,300 billion euros. Interest on that debt is becoming one of the biggest items in the national budget. Our hospitals are collapsing despite record funding. Our schools rank lower every year. Young people with degrees can’t afford an apartment in the city they were born in. Our best engineers leave for London, Zurich and San Francisco. And the rich you wanted to tax? They left too, and took the jobs with them.

The promise was protection. The result is stagnation.

The worst part is that nobody in France voted for decline. Every single step sounded generous, compassionate, reasonable. One more program. One more regulation. One more tax to fund it. Each step alone makes sense. Fifty years of them, and you wake up in a country that can no longer build a nuclear plant on time or keep its streets safe.

I love America because it’s the one place on earth where people still believe they can build something from nothing. I came to Silicon Valley as a self-taught kid and it changed my life. That spirit is the most precious thing your country has.

Before you vote, ask yourself one question: is the program you’re voting for making America more like America, or more like France?

Trust me. You don’t want to be France.

Breaking: #Eagles QB Jalen Hurts is out for Sunday due to a superficial blood clot. 

Full statement from the #Eagles on QB Jalen Hurts:
 
“On Thursday, October 8th, Jalen visited the training room after practice requesting treatment for his calf. He informed the medical staff he had been cleated during the Rams game on October 4th. This was his first treatment session for the calf injury following the game, after having practiced in full both Wednesday and Thursday. On Friday, Jalen received treatment, practiced in full, and was added to the practice report.
 
“Out of an abundance of caution, an ultrasound was performed on Saturday following the team’s flight to London and walkthrough. The ultrasound revealed a superficial blood clot. Our medical staff and doctors in London reviewed the results and concluded that activity and mobility were important and that Jalen could safely play. Doctors recommended a follow-up ultrasound within 72 hours of the game and the return flight to Philadelphia. 
 
“Jalen played without limitation in the game Sunday, received treatment on Monday and Tuesday, and practiced in full on Wednesday, as reflected in the practice report. Throughout our time in London and this week, we have remained in communication with the league office regarding the matter.  
 
"On Wednesday night, a follow-up ultrasound revealed movement in the small blood clot. Jalen will be out for Sunday’s game vs. the Panthers as we determine the appropriate course of treatment. His health and safety are our highest priority.”

posts.text:
In July 1989, 3-month-old Ryan Stallings became so sick that his parents rushed him to a hospital in St. Louis.

Tests found antifreeze in his blood.

Doctors believed he had been poisoned, so Ryan was taken from his parents and placed in foster care. From then on, they could only see him during short, supervised visits.

In early September, just days after a visit in which his mother, Patricia, fed him a bottle, Ryan fell ill again. Police found antifreeze in the family's basement and arrested Patricia. On September 7, Ryan died.

At the time, Patricia was pregnant. In February 1990, while she was waiting for trial, she gave birth to a second son, David Jr. He was taken from her right away.

Soon, David Jr. developed the same symptoms, even though he had never been in his mother's care. This time, doctors found the real cause: a rare genetic disorder called methylmalonic acidemia, which can look like antifreeze poisoning on lab tests.

Even so, in January 1991, a jury convicted Patricia of first-degree murder, and she was sentenced to life in prison.

Months later, her story aired on "Unsolved Mysteries." A scientist watching the episode retested Ryan's blood and found no antifreeze at all. Ryan had suffered from the same disorder as his little brother.

In September 1991, prosecutors dropped the charges and apologized. Patricia had spent nearly two years behind bars for a crime that never happened.
